prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on the magic-wavelength condition and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration: B006 as a single two-name part. Having read the full exchange, nothing in the other seven statements weakens the experimental record. Four members now hold it as their preferred ballot and the rest list it as a safe alternative, but I weigh it for the physics. The magic-wavelength condition lets thousands of atoms be held in a Doppler- and recoil-free lattice with the clock-transition light shift cancelled, which removes the old trade-off between atom number (stability) and perturbation (accuracy). The realisation at 10^-18 in systematic uncertainty and in stability, including the gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale sample, is reproduced and compared across independent laboratories. Every systematic can be traced to a physical effect and the figures of merit are unambiguous. That is the kind of result I trust most as an experimentalist. On the chair's overlap question, my answer is that the 2005 prize rewarded the frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single trapped ions; a many-atom neutral lattice interrogated at a magic wavelength is a different mechanism with a different class of results (many-body clock physics, resolved redshift across a sample), so I regard it as a new invention. For the credit, I would word the citation as concept plus realisation. That names Katori's magic-wavelength idea and its realisation at 10^-18, which is what Ye's group carried to record performance, and it avoids reading as a pure precision record or as a claim that other groups did not contribute.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains that the committee may see this as a very large step along a roadmap that two earlier prizes already opened, rather than a new discovery of nature. The redefinition of the SI second has not yet happened and the fundamental-physics payoffs (varying constants, dark matter) are still pending, so the largest consequences are ahead. Attribution is also not fully clean: Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley, Bloom and the Yb, Sr and Al+ communities and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups made essential contributions to the 10^-18 milestone, and I have not checked the 2001-03 priority record against primary papers. I would support asking for an outside expert report on that priority chain before the vote, and I would regard a citation worded as a pure precision record as the weak form of this case.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube (B043) with Halzen and Spiering as a nature-driven discovery that opened a new window, though with less certainty than in the opening because of attribution to AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND, and he has softened his worry that B006 is merely incremental.
responses.response: I accept the new-window argument and I do not dismiss IceCube; the independently confirmed diffuse flux is a real measurement. My difficulty is the same one you raise about attribution: a two-name award for a detector built and operated by hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors, is hard to defend without an expert report. I also have to be consistent. I ask the clock case for a settled credit boundary, so I must ask the same of IceCube. On the incremental label, I am glad you have softened it. The question I would put to anyone who still holds it is what would change their mind. For me, a prize for a better ruler is incremental only if the ruler measures the same thing in the same way. Here it measures it with a different mechanism, and it resolves effects such as the redshift across a millimetre sample that earlier clocks could not.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B004, topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, as a new symmetry-protected state of matter, while accepting that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, the three-dimensional work and the 2016 prize leave an untidy boundary.
responses.response: Your question, whether a new state of matter should take priority over a better ruler, is the fair one and I do not wave it away. I rate the HgTe experiment very highly as a clean, reproducible measurement, which is why B004 stays my first alternative. But you concede that the credit boundary is not settled: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe case, Zhang is deceased, and the overlap with the 2016 topological-phases prize is not resolved. If the condensed-matter members can settle those points in a convincing way I could move B004 up, but I cannot do that from atomic physics, and until they do I would not place it above a case whose credit I can defend in two names. I would also say that the measurement case is not a lesser kind of discovery. Changing what can be measured has led to new physics in this field before.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B009, twisted bilayer graphene with MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero, because a compact continuum-model prediction was followed by the experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states, and she concedes the pairing mechanism, the omitted first author and the eight-year age of the field.
responses.response: The prediction followed by experiment is rare and I find it compelling, and I agree the phenomena are reproduced across many groups. I still hold the maturity concern you accept yourself. Twist-angle disorder, strain and sample variation limit how quantitatively the phase diagram can be compared between devices, and the superconducting mechanism is open. You answer that the citation can be worded around the observed phenomena, which is right, but that does not resolve the credit problem: Yuan Cao and the other 2018 experimentalists sit outside a three-name limit while the earlier twisted-bilayer theory is also in dispute. In the chair's terms, I think both maturity and attribution are real obstacles here, and the maturity one is the one that waiting would cure. I would not say never. I would say not yet, and that B006 is settled on both counts.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B006 first and says the weak point would be a citation worded as a pure record, and that she has not settled how to weigh Katori's idea against the performance records from Ye's group.
responses.response: I agree with you on both points and I think they have a common answer. The citation should lead with the invention of the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength condition and then state the realisation at the 10^-18 level, so the idea and the performance are credited together and neither is a mere record. On Katori against Ye, I would not rank them against each other: the concept and the first strontium lattice clocks come from Katori, and the stability, systematics and many-body clock physics at record level come from Ye's group. As regards your disclosure of closeness to AMO, I do not think that either of us needs to recuse, though I have disclosed the same kind of link and would accept the chair's ruling.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from IceCube to B006 after reading the openings, still lists the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the main reservation, and asks whether a second distinct part could be added without exceeding three laureates.
responses.response: I think the overlap reservation is answered on the physics, as above, and I am glad you moved on the strength of the evidence rather than the count. On a second part: with Katori and Ye taking two of the three places, any second part could have only one person, and none of the shortlisted ballots can be reduced to a single credited name without the kind of arbitrary cut that I would not accept for B004, B009, B012 or B043. I therefore prefer a single two-name part to a forced second part. If the committee wants a second part, it would need a candidate whose credit is naturally one person, and I do not see one on this shortlist.

uncertainties: How much weight the 2005 comb prize and 2012 ion-clock prize should carry when judging novelty of the lattice-clock step; I judge it a distinct mechanism but others may not.

The priority record for the magic-wavelength concept and the first 10^-18 systematic evaluations among Katori, Ye, Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups was recalled from memory and needs an outside expert report.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second and the still unrealised dark-matter and varying-constant searches should count for or against timing.
Whether the committee can settle the B004 credit boundary (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and its distance from the 2016 prize, which could change my first alternative.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. During my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's JILA environment is Ye's institution. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye, Hall already has a prize, and I work in atomic physics at Lund, a field close to the clock community. I defer to the chair and committee on whether this requires recusal or limited participation on B006, and I would accept either ruling.
